repos.title: RAG-Anything: All-in-One RAG Framework
repos.paper_summary: RAG-Anything is a unified multimodal retrieval-augmented generation framework that builds a dual graph over documents: a cross-modal graph anchored on non-text units (figures, tables, equations) and a text-based graph, merged by entity-name alignment. Retrieval combines graph neighborhood expansion with dense embedding search over entities, relations, and chunks, and a VLM answers using text context plus the dereferenced visual content. On DocBench, it reaches 63.4% overall accuracy versus 61.0% for MMGraphRAG, 58.4% for LightRAG, and 51.2% for GPT-4o-mini. On MMLongBench, it reaches 42.8% versus 38.9% for LightRAG and 37.7% for MMGraphRAG. The gap grows with document length: on DocBench it is over 13 points for documents over 100 pages. Ablations on DocBench show 60.0% for chunk-only retrieval and 62.4% without the reranker, against 63.4% for the full system. All baselines use GPT-4o-mini, and accuracy is judged by GPT-4o-mini. The paper reports no variance across runs. Evaluation covers two benchmarks only.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems handle only text, so multimodal documents are poorly served; the paper proposes RAG-Anything to fix this.

digest_headlines.heading: The RAG-Anything Framework
digest_headlines.headline: RAG-Anything decomposes documents into typed units, builds two linked graphs, and retrieves through both structure and embeddings.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On MMLongBench, RAG-Anything scores 42.8% overall versus 37.7% for MMGraphRAG, with gains growing on longer documents.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work groups graph-enhanced RAG and multimodal RAG, and argues that prior multimodal systems fragment by modality.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that dual-graph retrieval helps long documents and identifies text-centric bias and rigid spatial processing as failure modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, extra case studies, the three multimodal prompts, the accuracy prompt, and failure-case analyses.

repos.title: Fast Graph Representation Learning with PyTorch Geometric
repos.paper_summary: PyTorch Geometric is a PyTorch library for deep learning on graphs, point clouds, and manifolds that implements a unified message-passing interface using sparse GPU acceleration. It represents graphs as node feature matrices and sparse adjacency tuples in COO format, performing neighborhood aggregation via vectorized gather and scatter operations rather than sparse matrix multiplication. The paper reports semi-supervised node classification accuracies of 83.1% to 83.3% on Cora with fixed splits and 75.8% to 79.4% with random splits across methods including GAT, GCN, and APPNP. Graph classification experiments on MUTAG, PROTEINS, COLLAB, IMDB-BINARY, and REDDIT-BINARY show GIN achieving the best flat performance, while DiffPool yields 92.1% accuracy on REDDIT-BINARY. Point cloud classification on ModelNet10 ranges from 92.07% to 93.28%, with PointCNN scoring highest. Runtime comparisons against DGL v0.2 indicate PyG trains up to 40 times faster using degree bucketing and up to 7 times faster than DGL's gather-scatter optimization for GAT. A stated limitation is that scatter operations are non-deterministic on GPUs, causing training results to vary across identical seeds, though inference remains stable.

repos.title: TokenPilot: Cache-Efficient Context Management for LLM Agents
repos.paper_summary:
TokenPilot is a context management framework for LLM agents that reduces inference costs by aligning text compression with prompt cache continuity. It operates at two granularities: Ingestion-Aware Compaction stabilizes the prompt prefix by replacing volatile runtime variables with static placeholders and stripping structural noise from tool responses before they enter the context window; Lifecycle-Aware Eviction monitors context segments in batches, offloading them only when their estimated residual utility expires. This prevents the layout mutations that typically invalidate hardware KV caches.

Evaluated on PinchBench (123 tasks) and Claw-Eval (161 tasks) using GPT-5.4-mini, TokenPilot reduces total inference cost by 61% and 56% in isolated mode, and 61% and 87% in continuous mode, respectively, while maintaining competitive task accuracy. For instance, on Claw-Eval continuous mode, it lowers cost from USD 81.52 to USD 10.58. The system requires backend support for prefix caching and relies on a model-based estimator that may misclassify segments under ambiguous interaction patterns. Additionally, performance gains depend on grouping same-category tasks into contiguous sessions, as heterogeneous streams exhibit lower prefix reuse rates due to frequent tool schema changes.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Text pruning cuts tokens but mutates prompt layouts and breaks cache reuse, so TokenPilot pairs ingestion stabilization with lifecycle eviction.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Serving cost is modeled as discounted cache-hit tokens plus full-cost miss tokens across isolated and continuous task modes.

digest_headlines.heading: TokenPilot
digest_headlines.headline: The framework stabilizes prompt prefixes at ingestion and evicts context segments only after their residual utility expires, in batches of turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On Claw-Eval isolated mode, TokenPilot scores 63.1 at USD 2.27 cost, versus Vanilla's 64.5 at USD 5.16.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers static text compression, passive memory retrieval and summarization, and runtime paging and scheduling of context.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion states that TokenPilot cuts inference cost in both modes without sacrificing task effectiveness.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limits include estimator misclassification, tuning of threshold tau and batch size, dependence on prefix caching, and weaker reuse on shuffled streams.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists benchmark statistics, cost formula and prices, baseline settings, hyperparameters, estimator prompts, and mixed-category results.

repos.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
repos.paper_summary: Harness2 is a plug-and-play framework for recursive agent harnessing. It refines an LLM agent's execution harness (its prompts, memory, skills, tools, and related components) for each task, and it updates a separate improvement harness across tasks. Task-level recursion uses a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step. It proposes harness edits, runs them under matched conditions against a reference execution, and composes only changes supported by behavioral contrasts, without a ground-truth verifier. Parallel recursion composes from a pool of candidates, and sequential recursion chains revisions. Both are controlled by a budget k. After each task, reflection adds adopted harnesses and supported lessons to a library that guides later proposals. On WorkBuddy-Bench, JobBench, and LAB (Partial pass rate), with Gemini 3.5 Flash and GLM-5 under OpenCode and Codex, one step improves every configuration by up to 11.5 points, 4.5 points, and 11.8 percentage points. Parallel recursion at k=5 adds up to 3.9, 4.2, and 6.7 more. The authors state that probe contrasts are limited by execution stochasticity and shared model biases, and that adopted harnesses are not verified to be optimal.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 targets open-world agent harness evolution, which lacks ground-truth verifiers and fails to transfer across tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Harness2
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 pairs task-level recursion, which refines the current harness without verifiers, with a library that carries lessons to later tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Single-step Harness2 exceeds the base harness on all three benchmarks for GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash under both initial harnesses.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Score gains grow with recursion budget, and each ablated component lowers WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 differs from prior harness optimization by learning from its own refinements across a task stream without ground-truth feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 turns task-specific refinement into reusable experience, with gains reported across three benchmarks, two executors, and two initial harnesses.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers comparison criteria, benchmark splits, baselines, tool-call errors, production harness comparison, failure cases, limitations, and prompts.

repos.title: GaussianAvatar: Towards Realistic Human Avatar Modeling from a Single Video via Animatable 3D Gaussians
repos.paper_summary:
GaussianAvatar reconstructs animatable human avatars from a single monocular video using 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method represents the human body as a set of canonical 3D Gaussians that are reposed to arbitrary poses via forward skinning, bypassing the inverse skinning ambiguity inherent in NeRF-based approaches. A dynamic appearance network, combined with an optimizable feature tensor, predicts pose-dependent properties such as surface offsets and colors to capture cloth wrinkles. Because the rendering is differentiable with respect to motion parameters, the system jointly optimizes SMPL pose estimates and avatar appearance during training, correcting inaccuracies in initial monocular motion tracking.

On the People-Snapshot dataset, the full model achieves a PSNR of 30.98 dB, outperforming InstantAvatar (29.53 dB) and HumanNeRF (26.90 dB). On the more challenging DynVideo dataset, it reaches 28.58 dB PSNR compared to 20.31 dB for InstantAvatar. Rendering speed is 35 FPS, significantly faster than the 3.87 FPS of InstantAvatar. The authors note that inaccurate foreground segmentation can cause boundary artifacts, and the method struggles to model loose garments like dresses due to reliance on standard SMPL skinning weights.

repos.title: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
repos.paper_summary:
Prime Agent is an open-source harness for long-horizon evaluation and coding-agent workflows. It provides a persistent IPython REPL, recursive subagents with direct agent-to-agent communication, and Continual Harness for storing versioned prompts, memories, skills, and subagent specifications across trajectories. The model controls strategy construction while the runtime standardizes execution, recovery, and resource accounting.

The paper evaluates Prime Agent against native and alternative harnesses (Pi, Claude Code, Codex) on interactive reasoning, long-context tasks, and autonomous systems construction. On ARC-AGI-3, Prime Agent raises RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5%. In long-context benchmarks, it matches or exceeds baselines; for example, on OOLONG (Yahoo, 128k), GPT-5.6 Sol scores .940 with Prime Agent versus .900 with Codex. For GPU kernel generation on PMPP-Hard, Prime Agent achieves comparable solve rates at substantially reduced token cost. A seven-day Factorio run completed 24 of 196 technologies using 23.4 million output tokens. Limitations include models' poor handling of irreversible actions and online refinement potentially preserving specification exploits as reusable skills.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent argues the harness should expose expressive primitives, so evaluation measures model capability rather than harness failures.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Prime Agent Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent splits information management from computation management across persistent sessions, a daemon and Continual Harness state.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent is generally competitive on long-context tasks and close to native harnesses on GPU-kernel generation.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work spans programmatic inference, coding-agent runtimes, ARC-AGI-3 systems and multi-agent communication, which Prime Agent combines.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Many harness capabilities remain underused because current models were not trained to operate them.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists three out-of-loop nanoGPT experiments, from Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro and a third model, plus an orchestration example.

repos.title: Qwen Technical Report
repos.paper_summary:
The Qwen technical report releases a series of large language models, including base models (1.8B, 7B, and 14B parameters), aligned chat models, and specialized variants for coding and mathematics. The base models are pretrained on up to 33 trillion tokens using a modified Transformer architecture with RoPE positional embeddings and RMSNorm. Alignment involves supervised finetuning followed by reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) using Proximal Policy Optimization.

On standard benchmarks, the 14B base model achieves 66.3% on MMLU (5-shot) and 61.3% on GSM8K (8-shot), outperforming larger open-source models like Llama 2-70B in several tasks. The aligned 14B chat model scores 66.5% on MMLU (5-shot) and 43.9% on HumanEval (0-shot). In human evaluations against GPT-3.5, the RLHF-aligned 14B model wins more frequently than its SFT counterpart but still trails GPT-4. Specialized Code-Qwen models reach 32.3% pass@1 on HumanEval, while Math-Qwen-Chat approaches GPT-3.5 performance on GSM8K. Limitations include the reliance on proprietary benchmarks for tool-use evaluation and the continued performance gap relative to GPT-4 in complex reasoning and creative writing tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen is a series of base, chat, coding and math language models, with the 14B and 7B base and chat models released openly.

digest_headlines.heading: Pretraining
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen base models trained on up to 3 trillion tokens are compared with open-source baselines on 7 benchmarks, with extended-context perplexity reported.

digest_headlines.heading: Alignment
digest_headlines.headline: Chat models are aligned by supervised finetuning and RLHF, with Qwen-14B-Chat trailing only ChatGPT and Llama 2-Chat-70B on the reported benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Code-Qwen: Specialized Model for Coding
digest_headlines.headline: Code-Qwen continues pretraining Qwen on about 90 billion code tokens, reaching 66.4 pass@1 on HumanEval for the 14B chat model.

digest_headlines.heading: Math-Qwen: Specialized Model for Mathematics Reasoning
digest_headlines.headline: Math-Qwen-Chat 14B scores 69.8 on grade-school math problems and 24.2 on competition math, against 60.1 and 18.4 for Qwen-Chat 14B.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers large model scaling, open-source chat models, tool-use agents, code models and math reasoning methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen's report concludes that its models are competitive with open-source models and match some proprietary models on benchmarks and human evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the chat data format, automatic evaluation tables for examination, knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, and human evaluation cases.

repos.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
repos.paper_summary:
Mamba is a sequence model architecture that replaces Transformer attention with selective state space models (SSMs) to achieve linear-time scaling. The method makes SSM parameters $\Delta$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ functions of the input, allowing the model to selectively propagate or forget information based on content. Because this input-dependency prevents standard convolutional computation, the authors implement a hardware-aware parallel scan algorithm that performs discretization and recurrence in GPU SRAM rather than HBM, using recomputation during backpropagation to limit memory usage.

The architecture combines the SSM layer and MLP into a single block without attention. On language modeling tasks, Mamba-3B outperforms Pythia-3B by 4 points on average common sense reasoning and matches the performance of Pythia-7B. It achieves 5x higher generation throughput than comparable Transformers. For audio and genomics, Mamba reduces FID scores by more than half compared to baselines like Hyena and SaShiMi. The paper notes that evaluation was limited to models below 7B parameters and that the selection mechanism may reduce performance on continuous data modalities where linear time-invariant SSMs excel.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Transformers are costly on long sequences, and Mamba adds input-dependent state space dynamics that scale linearly and match Transformers on language.

digest_headlines.heading: State Space Models
digest_headlines.headline: Structured state space models are linear time-invariant, so their parameters stay fixed across time steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Selective State Space Models
digest_headlines.headline: Selection lets SSM parameters depend on the input, which breaks convolution, so a hardware-aware scan computes the model efficiently.

digest_headlines.heading: Empirical Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show Mamba solves synthetic recall tasks and outperforms baselines on language, DNA and audio, with 5× higher throughput.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Selective SSMs trade off on continuous data such as audio, and scaling beyond small sizes remains unassessed.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Mamba is a strong candidate for a general sequence backbone, with selection giving context-dependent reasoning at linear scaling in length.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers selection versus gating, related work, speech-generation training details, and efficiency benchmarks.

repos.title: Datasets: A Community Library for Natural Language Processing
repos.paper_summary: **Datasets** is a community library for NLP that standardizes the interface, versioning, and documentation for text datasets. The library uses a distributed approach where community-contributed builder modules download raw data from original hosts and convert it into a typed tabular format backed by Apache Arrow. This architecture allows memory-mapped access to small or internet-scale corpora without loading them entirely into RAM. It includes a `map` function for parallel processing and supports streaming for datasets too large for disk. A Dataset Hub provides structured tags and "data cards" to document dataset properties, licensing, and known biases. After one year of development, the library contains 681 unique datasets with over 250 contributors. Use cases include the Eleuther AI evaluation harness for nearly 100 tasks and the GEM shared task covering 12 NLG datasets. Limitations include reliance on external hosting, which means removed datasets become unavailable, and the need for manual curation of data cards, which may lag behind new findings regarding annotation artifacts or social biases.

repos.title: Unity: A General Platform for Intelligent Agents
repos.paper_summary: The paper introduces a four-category taxonomy for reinforcement learning simulation platforms and identifies the Unity engine with the open-source ML-Agents Toolkit as a general platform capable of supporting arbitrary visual, physical, task-logic, and social complexity. The toolkit provides a Python API using gRPC to control Unity scenes, exposing runtime parameters for curriculum learning and domain randomization. It includes implementations of PPO, SAC, GAIL, and behavioral cloning, along with fourteen example environments. Performance benchmarks show `env.step()` latencies ranging from 0.803 ms for a single vector observation to 9.23 ms for four visual agents. On the Obstacle Tower benchmark, baseline RL agents solved an average of five floors after 20 million steps, while the top competition entry solved 19.4 floors, surpassing naive human performance but remaining below expert levels. The paper notes that high-fidelity rendering increases memory overhead compared to lightweight simulators like MuJoCo, and that hyperparameter tuning remains a significant barrier for non-expert users despite the provided graphical editor.
